t.3.65.2: And Bhīma, having given them abundant wealth, instructed them: "Search for Nala, and for my daughter Damayantī as well."
t.3.65.1: When Nala, his kingdom taken, had fallen into servitude along with his wife, Bhīma sent forth brahmins, longing to see Nala.
t.3.65.3: When this task is accomplished and the lord of the Niṣadhas has been found, I will give a thousand cows to whichever of you brings those two back, and I will also give him an agrahāra, a village equal to a town.
t.3.65.4: If Damayantī or Nala cannot be brought here, then even upon their merely being found I will give a wealth of a thousand cows.
t.3.65.5: Thus addressed, those brāhmaṇas went forth joyfully in every direction, searching through cities and kingdoms for the Naiṣadha together with his wife.
t.3.65.7: He saw her, her matchless beauty only dimly discernible, like the radiance of fire veiled by a net of smoke.
t.3.65.6: Then a brahmin named Sudeva, searching for the Vaidarbhī, came to the lovely city of the Cedis and saw her in the king's palace, standing with Sunandā during the king's puṇyāhavācana ceremony.
t.3.65.8: Seeing her, the large-eyed woman, exceedingly soiled and emaciated, he surmised, “This is Bhaimī,” confirming it by various signs.
t.3.65.9: Just as I saw her before, so does this woman appear now. Having seen her today, like Śrī herself, beloved of the world, I have achieved my purpose.
t.3.65.10: He saw the dark-hued queen, her face like the full moon and her breasts lovely and round, who with her radiance made all the directions free of darkness.
t.3.65.11: Her whose eyes were like the petals of a lovely lotus, who was like Rati, the consort of Manmatha, dear to the whole world, like the radiance of the full moon.
t.3.65.13: Like a full-moon night whose moon has been swallowed by Rāhu, she was distraught with grief for her husband and wretched, like a river whose streams have dried up.
t.3.65.12: Her, like a lotus stalk plucked from that lake of Vidarbha as if by the fault of fate, her limbs thickly smeared with dirt and mire.
t.3.65.14: She was like a troubled lotus pond, its leaves and lotuses torn apart, its birds frightened away, crushed by the trunk of an elephant.
t.3.65.15: Her, so delicate, of finely formed limbs, accustomed to chambers filled with jewels, now seemingly scorched by the heat, like a lotus stalk freshly pulled from the water.
t.3.65.16: Her, endowed with beauty, nobility and virtues, worthy of ornaments yet unadorned, like the new crescent of the moon in the sky veiled by dark clouds.
t.3.65.17: She is bereft of the dear pleasures of love and bereft of her kinsfolk, a wretched woman who sustains her body only out of longing to see her husband.
t.3.65.18: A husband, indeed, is the highest ornament of a woman, even without ornaments; separated from him, this woman, though beautiful, does not shine.
t.3.65.19: Nala does an exceedingly difficult thing, in that, though bereft of her, he still sustains his own body and does not sink down in grief.
t.3.65.20: Seeing her, with the ends of her hair so black and her eyes long as hundred-petalled lotuses, worthy of happiness yet now in sorrow, even my mind is troubled.
t.3.65.21: When indeed will this lovely and virtuous woman reach the far shore of her sorrow through union with her husband, as Rohiṇī does through union with the moon?
t.3.65.22: Surely the Naiṣadha will find joy in regaining her, like a king who, having fallen from his kingdom, has won back the earth once more.
t.3.65.23: The Naiṣadha is worthy of the Vaidarbhī, who is endowed with equal character and age and joined with equal lineage, and this black-eyed one is worthy of him.
t.3.65.24: It is fitting for me to console the wife of that immeasurable man, endowed with valor and courage, who longs to see her husband.
t.3.65.25: Here I am; I shall console her, whose face is like the full moon, who had never before known sorrow, and who is now stricken with grief and lost in brooding thought.
t.3.65.26: Bṛhadaśva said: Having thus considered her by various reasons and distinguishing marks, the brāhmaṇa Sudeva then approached Bhaimī and spoke.
t.3.65.27: I am Sudeva, O Vaidarbhī, the dear friend of your brother; at the word of King Bhīma I have come here to search for you.
t.3.65.28: Your father is well, O queen, and so are your mother and your brothers; your two children who dwell there are also well and long-lived. But on your account all your kinsfolk sit as though their very life had left them.
t.3.65.29: Recognizing Sudeva, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Damayantī then asked him in turn about all her own friends and kinsfolk.
t.3.65.30: And the princess of Vidarbha, worn down by grief, wept bitterly, O king, when she suddenly saw Sudeva, that best of twice-born men, dear to her brother.
t.3.65.31: Then, O Bhārata, Sunandā saw her weeping, worn down by grief, and speaking with Sudeva in private.
t.3.65.33: Then the mother of the lord of the Cedis, the king, went from the inner apartments of the palace to where that young woman was with the brāhmaṇa.
t.3.65.32: She sent word to her mother: “Having met with a brāhmaṇa, the sairandhrī is weeping bitterly. He knows her, if you think it worth considering.”
t.3.65.34: Then, lord of the people, the queen mother had Sudeva brought before her and asked: "Whose wife is this beautiful lady, or whose daughter?"
t.3.65.35: And how did this lovely-eyed woman become lost to her kinsmen or to her husband? And how, O brahmin, was this virtuous lady recognized by you when she had come to such a state?
t.3.65.36: I wish to learn all of this from you, completely and without omission. Tell me truly, for I am asking you about this woman of divine form.
t.3.65.37: Thus addressed by her, O king, Sudeva, best of the twice-born, sat comfortably and recounted the story of Damayantī exactly as it had happened.
